newsitem.title: KUWAIT: New Kuwait cabinet has four elected MPs.
newsitem.headline: New Kuwait cabinet has four elected MPs.

text.p: Kuwait has formed a new cabinet which is expected to muster a majority in parliament after four years of clashes with the former opposition-dominated house.

The 14-man government announced on Tuesday night includes four elected members of parliament. The other 10 are by law ex- officio MPs -- further boosting the cabinet's sway in the new all-male parliament which was elected last week.

Analysts earlier said up to 19 of the new MPs were pro- government, Shi'ite and Sunni Moslem fundamentalists and pro- Islamists secured about 14 seats, six seats are held by liberals while the rest is shared by independents and tribal MPs.
Pro-Islamist MP Nasser al-Sanea dismissed claims that the new parliament would be tamer than the last one, in which he also served. "The new parliament still has (an opposition) flare".
Some politicians say the small but vocal liberal opposition group and many Islamists could give the government some headaches.

The last house was no rubber stamp organisation, opening wide probes into alleged official corruption and misuse of public funds. It also questioned arms deals with Western allies and the state's management of events prior to Iraq's 1990-91 occupation of the tiny state.
The new parliament, the only elected house in a Gulf Arab state, holds its first session on October 20.
About 35 of the 50 elected MPs met on Monday to discuss their role in the new parliament and government.
But "there were differences...a group wanted MPs to hold up to eight ministries with a minimum of six, others favoured a lesser role," an MP who attended the meeting told Reuters.
According to the constitution, at least one elected MP has to join the cabinet. The last government had four elected MPs while the previous one had a record six.

"I think that the experience of elected MPs becoming ministers has been successful. I was expecting the numbers to increase and not to decrease," said Abdul-Mohsen al-Mudej, who resigned as oil minister in September to seek re-election.
U.S.-educated Issa Mazeedi, a member of Kuwait's Shi'ite minority, was made oil minister in the cabinet which is once again headed by Crown Prince Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah.
The last cabinet also had one Shi'ite.
The main lines of oil policy in OPEC heavyweight Kuwait, with a current daily output of about two million barrels, is decided by the Supreme Petroleum Council, headed by Sheikh Saad.

"We as deputies have specific aspirations...The main issues are security, restructuring the economy, boosting deteriorating services and the emerging unemployment problem," MP Mudej told Reuters after the cabinet was named.
In addition to Sheikh Saad, the new cabinet includes four other members of the ruling al-Sabah family.
Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah, a brother to the Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah, was re-named first deputy prime minister and Foreign Minister, an official decree said.

Nasser Abdulla al-Rodhan kept his post as Finance Minister and is one of three deputy prime ministers. The other deputy is Sheikh Salem Sabah al-Salem al-Sabah, a former foreign minister, who was named new defence minister.

Sheikh Mohammad Khaled al-Hamad al-Sabah, also a member of the ruling family, was made new Interior Minister while Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah, who served as ambassador to Washington during the Gulf crisis, kept the Information Ministry. He is also acting health minister.
